items.title: conv2d: group-aware L1 weight estimate for grouped/depthwise conv
items.body:
## Problem

`calculate_L1_usage_for_conv_op()` estimated conv weight memory as `in_channels × kh × kw × out_channels` regardless of `groups`. For grouped/depthwise convolutions the actual weight tensor is `out_channels × (in_channels/groups) × kh × kw`.

At C=10240, groups=10240, K=4 that overstates weights by ~10,000× (~838 MB vs ~80 KB) and the DRAM auto-slicer reports no valid config.

## Change

When `groups > 1`, divide `in_channels_aligned` by `groups` before building the weight-shape estimate. `groups == 1` is unchanged.

## Silicon (2× Blackhole p150a)

| Shape | Result |
|---|---|
| C=2560 bf16 | PASS PCC 0.999994 |
| C=5120 bf8 | PASS PCC 0.999824 |
| C=64 bf16 | PASS PCC 0.999993 |
| C=5120 bf16 | still no valid DRAM slice (real CBs, not estimate) |
| C=10240 bf16 | same — true per-core L1 capacity, T=12 cannot be width-sliced |

Regression test is C=2560, the largest bf16 shape we ran to completion. This PR is an estimate correction, not a C=10240 capacity fix. It does not close #53303.

Refs #53303

items.title: ttnn.conv1d depthwise conv (groups=10240) hits TT_FATAL in DRAM auto-slice: group-blind L1 weights estimate
items.body:
## Title

`ttnn.conv1d` depthwise conv (groups=10240) hits TT_FATAL in DRAM auto-slice: group-blind L1 weights estimate

## Environment

- pjrt-plugin-tt 1.4.0 wheel — commit `941a6b866a9284cadd4b33e3c4b0dc973b3e8ba5`, built 2026-07-23 (release)
  - tt-metal `f1f4ff75579ebd7a69c7da52d45368f273026d85`
  - tt-mlir `6b2d83bbee7bc60e8521b814368d32785df6cd73`
- torch 2.11.0+cpu, torch-xla 2.9.0+git56f8e61, transformers 5.15.0
- 2x Blackhole, opened as a 1x2 mesh (`ttnn.open_mesh_device(ttnn.MeshShape(1, 2))`)
- Same TT_FATAL with pure BF16 activations/weights and with BFP8_B experimental weights — not a dtype-conversion issue.

## Observed

During device execution of a Qwen3.5 GDN block's causal depthwise `conv1d`
(C=10240, kernel 4, seq len 12, i.e. conv2d with input `[1, 1, 12, 10240]`, weight
`[10240, 1, 1, 4]`, groups=10240, padding 3), the op aborts:

```
warning  | Op | Conv2D DRAM doesn't support specifying memory config, as the output will always be DRAM Interleaved (conv2d.cpp:806)
warning  | Op | Failed to find valid config with height-slicing. Attempting fallback to width-slicing. (op_slicing.cpp:233)
critical | TT_FATAL: DRAM Auto slice could not find valid slice configuration. Tried up to 1 slices for width-slicing on output dimension 15. Available L1: 1395456 bytes. Operation requires more memory than available even with maximum slicing. (assert.hpp:104)
{TT_FATAL @ ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/sliding_window/op_slicing/op_slicing.cpp:266: found_valid_config
```

Abridged stack (demangled):

```
ttnn::operations::op_slicing::run_sliced_op(...)
ttnn::operations::conv::conv2d::conv2d_DRAM(...)
ttnn::conv2d(...)
ttnn::conv1d(...)
tt::runtime::ttnn::operations::conv::run(tt::target::ttnn::Conv1dOp const*, ...)
tt::runtime::ttnn::ProgramExecutor::execute()
tt::runtime::ttnn::submit(...) / tt::runtime::submit(...)
tt::pjrt::FlatbufferLoadedExecutableInstance::execute(...)
torch_xla::runtime::PjRtComputationClient::ExecuteReplicated(...)
```

Python surface (torch-xla lazy execution): `RuntimeError: Bad StatusOr access: INTERNAL: Error code: 13`.

## Reproduction

Minimal standalone (reproducer script attached):

```python
import torch, ttnn
from ttnn.types import Layout

C, K, T, PAD = 10240, 4, 12, 3   # depthwise causal: pad = K-1, output width = T+2*PAD-K+1 = 15
mesh = ttnn.open_mesh_device(ttnn.MeshShape(1, 2))
x = ttnn.from_torch(torch.randn(1, 1, T, C), dtype=ttnn.bfloat16, layout=Layout.ROW_MAJOR, device=mesh)
w = ttnn.from_torch(torch.randn(C, 1, 1, K), dtype=ttnn.bfloat16, layout=Layout.ROW_MAJOR, device=mesh)
out = ttnn.conv1d(x, w, mesh, in_channels=C, out_channels=C, batch_size=1,
                  input_length=T, kernel_size=K, stride=1, padding=PAD, dilation=1, groups=C)
out.cpu()
```

Verified: running the snippet above reproduces the fatal (2026-08-16, install per
Environment: pjrt-plugin-tt 1.4.0, tt-metal `f1f4ff75`, tt-mlir `6b2d83bb`,
python 3.12.13, torch 2.11.0+cpu; the script exits 0 by design when the fatal
is observed):

```text
warning  | Op | Failed to find valid config with height-slicing. Attempting fallback to width-slicing. (op_slicing.cpp:233)
critical | Always | TT_FATAL: DRAM Auto slice could not find valid slice configuration. Tried up to 1 slices for width-slicing on output dimension 15. Available L1: 1461504 bytes. Operation requires more memory than available even with maximum slicing. (assert.hpp:104)
```

Python surface (direct eager `ttnn.conv1d`, no PjRt layer):
`{TT_FATAL @ ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/sliding_window/op_slicing/op_slicing.cpp:266: found_valid_config}`.

Same assert site and fatal text as the torch-xla occurrence above. Only deltas:
the `conv2d.cpp:806` memory-config warning does not appear (it fires only when a
memory_config is explicitly passed — the runtime path passes one, the eager call
does not), and the available-L1 figure differs by 64.5 KiB (1461504 vs 1395456
bytes; call-path-dependent L1 accounting). Without the PjRt layer the exception
surfaces as the raw TT_FATAL instead of `Bad StatusOr … Error code 13`.

First seen through the torch-xla flow (tt-mlir-lowered GDN `conv1d`, 4-layer
model slice, tokens `[1, 12]`), same fatal for BF16 and BFP8_B weights.

## Analysis

Slicing geometry, consistent with the message:

- conv1d lowers to conv2d with H=1; padding 3 on W=12 gives output width
  `12 + 2*3 - 4 + 1 = 15` → "output dimension 15".
- H=1 admits at most 1 slice; W=15 with 32-wide tiles gives `div_up(15, 32) = 1`
  → "Tried up to 1 slices". Neither spatial axis can reduce the footprint: the
  memory driver is the channel count, which slicing never touches.

Root-cause hypothesis (analysis from tt-metal source at the commit above, not yet
confirmed on main): `calculate_L1_usage_for_conv_op`
(`ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/conv/conv2d/conv2d_utils.cpp:1007`, `weights_shape`
at :1051) builds the weights estimate as `{1, 1, in_ch*k*k, out_ch}` =
`{1, 1, 40960, 10240}` ≈ 838 MB in BF16 — i.e. it ignores `groups`. The true
depthwise weight tensor is `out_ch * (in_ch/groups) * kh * kw` = 40960 elements
≈ 80 KB. The group-blind estimate alone exceeds any slicing budget, producing
"Operation requires more memory than available even with maximum slicing" for a
conv whose real weights fit easily.

## Workarounds

- Replace the causal depthwise conv with an equivalent tap-shift + (grouped)
  matmul formulation; verified against `F.conv1d` on CPU with PCC 0.999989.
- tt-mlir main carries `GroupedConvChannelSplitRewritePattern`
  (`kMaxGroupedConvChannels = 4096`), which would split this grouped conv at the
  frontend before it reaches `ttnn.conv1d` as a single C=10240 op.

## Related

- #49793
- #49768
- #50475

## Suggested fix

Make the conv L1 usage estimate group-aware in `conv2d_utils.cpp`: when
`groups > 1`, the weight footprint per slice should be
`out_ch * (in_ch / groups) * kh * kw` elements rather than
`in_ch * kh * kw * out_ch`. With the corrected estimate this conv's real weight
footprint (~80 KB BF16) fits the per-core L1 budget and the slice search should
find a valid config (or run unsliced). Optionally, if the corrected estimate
still exceeds the device scale, fail early with a diagnostic that names the
estimated tensor sizes instead of a doomed "maximum slicing" search.

items.title: Gate Chunked Kimi perf (code_debug 55k, no trace) at +/-5% per chunk
items.body:
### Ticket
Closes #53287. Untraced counterpart of #53101 (traced twin, ±3%).

### Problem
`Blaze - Chunked Kimi perf (code_debug 55k, no trace)` printed its per-chunk timing table but never asserted on it — #53101 hard-wired the gate to `use_trace=True`, so a regression on the eager-dispatch path went green. The stated reason was that untraced within-run spread (~20%) is too wide to band. But that spread is *per-iteration*; the median of the 9 post-warmup iterations is stable, and that is what the gate uses.

### Calibration
Per-chunk `median_time` from every run of this job with a table, 2026-08-11 → 08-15 (32 runs, `bh_sc1_high_power`, many branches). Untraced is flat ~1.09 s/chunk — no depth ramp, the op2op gap swamps it.

Baseline = per chunk, the median over the 10 most recent green runs (2026-08-15, `main`): 31868565025 31868547288 31868532277 31868515545 31868482938 31868467067 31868452031 31868433473 31867986909 31866023124.

| worst single-chunk deviation | those 10 runs | all 32 runs |
|---|---|---|
| | 2.9% | **3.2%** |

Every per-chunk median ever recorded sits in 1.063–1.129 s (6.2% total spread). Replaying all 32 at **±5%: 0 would fail**, worst case using 64% of the band. The issue asked for ±10%; the data does not need it, so this ships the tighter bar and documents the escalation order beside the table — re-center on the midrange first (3.2% → 2.7%, the tail is one-sided), widen to 10% only after.

### Changes
- Split the baseline table by mode: `KIMI_TRACED_BASELINE_CHUNK_TIMES_S` (numbers untouched) + new `KIMI_UNTRACED_BASELINE_CHUNK_TIMES_S`, with `TRACED_PERF_MARGIN = 0.03` / `UNTRACED_PERF_MARGIN = 0.05`.
- `kimi_chunked_perf_gate()` replaces the inline `use_trace` fork and returns `(baseline, margin)`. Mode picks the table *and* the band, so #53101's structural guard survives — generalized from "untraced is never gated" to "each mode only sees its own numbers". `preload_isl > 0` and uncalibrated `(num_layers, n_chunks, num_iters)` stay record-only.
- `perf_margin` parametrizes as `None` = "mode default" (id `margin3pct` → `margin_auto`; no CI `-k` selector uses it); explicit values still override. `print_duration_table` now raises on baseline-without-margin instead of collapsing the band to zero width.

The accuracy test stays record-only — it has no `is_high_power()` skipif, so it can land on hardware the baselines never covered.

### Test plan
- [x] Gate resolution unit-checked over 8 parametrizations (both modes × calibrated/uncalibrated/preloaded + override).
- [x] All 32 historical runs replayed at ±5%: 0 failures.
- [x] CI, 4 runs x {untraced, traced}. All four **untraced** jobs pass; worst chunk uses 28-53% of the 5% band, matching the historical replay.

| run | ran with | untraced (this PR) | traced (unchanged, ±3%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [31929446467](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/actions/runs/31929446467) | ±5% | ✅ worst -2.4% | ✅ worst +0.8% |
| [31929452341](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/actions/runs/31929452341) | ±5% | ✅ worst +1.4% | ✅ worst +0.8% |
| [31929212372](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/actions/runs/31929212372) | ±10% | ✅ worst -1.7% *(inside ±5% too)* | ✅ worst +1.8% |
| [31929217523](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/actions/runs/31929217523) | ±10% | ✅ worst -2.7% *(inside ±5% too)* | ❌ worst +8.3%, 8/11 chunks out |

History was squashed to one commit after these ran. The only delta between what CI executed and `93d7faa` is the reverted `blaze_models_prefill_tests.yaml` comment edits — comments in a pipeline file, not executed by anything — so the results above still describe this code.

**The one red job is the traced gate, and it is pre-existing** — `TRACED_PERF_MARGIN` is 3% before and after this PR, and that job's numbers are unrelated to anything here. Run 31929217523's traced job drew a slow/noisy runner: per-chunk stddev 0.043-0.060 s against the usual ≤0.002 s, medians ramping 0.595 → 0.966 s, worst on the deep chunks (+7.2% chunk 9, +6.7% chunk 10) exactly as predicted when #53101 landed. Its own untraced twin in the same run passed with 2.7% to spare, and the traced job passed on the other three runs.

That is the traced gate's known ~1-in-4 exposure to the pool's slow profile, and the fix is the one this PR demonstrates for untraced: baseline traced off a median-of-N runs rather than the single run 31675454129, and/or give chunks 9-10 their own wider band. Out of scope here — filing separately rather than quietly widening someone else's gate.

items.title: Input validation via TT_ASSERT is a no-op in Release: polyval reads coeffs[0] out of bounds on an empty vector, complex_tensor loses shape validation entirely
items.body:
### Component / Area

ttnn eltwise host code — `binary/device/binary_composite_op.cpp` (`polyval`), `complex/complex.cpp` (`complex_tensor`), `ternary/ternary_composite_op.cpp` (`mac`)

### Issue Type (optional)

Bad Outputs

### Observed

Three user-facing entry points guard their inputs with `TT_ASSERT`, which is compiled out in
Release builds. `tt_stl/tt_stl/assert.hpp:155-168`:

```cpp
#ifdef DEBUG
#define TT_ASSERT(condition, ...) \
    do { if (not(condition)) [[unlikely]] tt::assert::detail::tt_assert(...); } while (0)
#else
#define TT_ASSERT(condition, ...) \
    do { (void)(condition); } while (0)   // no-op in Release
#endif
```

So in a Release build — which is what anyone runs — these checks do not exist. The three are not
equally severe; they are grouped because the cause is one and a fix would touch them together.

---

**1. `polyval` — out-of-bounds read on an empty coefficient vector. This is the one that matters.**

```cpp
// binary_composite_op.cpp:653-660
Tensor polyval(const Tensor& input_a, const std::vector<float>& coeffs, ...) {
    TT_ASSERT(!coeffs.empty() && "coeffs should be 1 or more coefficients");
    if (coeffs.size() == 1) {
        return ttnn::full_like(input_a, coeffs[0]);
    }
    Tensor result = ttnn::multiply(input_a, coeffs[0], ...);   // <-- coeffs[0] on an empty vector
```

`coeffs` comes straight from the caller. With `coeffs = {}` in a Release build the assert vanishes,
`size() == 1` is false, and `coeffs[0]` reads past the end of an empty `std::vector` — undefined
behaviour reached from ordinary Python-level input, not from an internal invariant.

There is a second latent problem on the next line, currently masked by the first:

```cpp
for (int idx = 1; idx < coeffs.size() - 1; idx++) {
```

`coeffs.size()` is `size_t`, so for an empty vector `coeffs.size() - 1` wraps to `SIZE_MAX`, and
the signed/unsigned comparison promotes `idx`. If the `coeffs[0]` read above were fixed without
touching this, the loop would still run away. Worth fixing both in one go.

The guard should be a `TT_FATAL` with an explicit message:

```cpp
-    TT_ASSERT(!coeffs.empty() && "coeffs should be 1 or more coefficients");
+    TT_FATAL(!coeffs.empty(), "polyval requires 1 or more coefficients, got 0");
```

(Minor, and stated so it is not overclaimed: the `&& "literal"` idiom folds the text into the
condition rather than passing it as the message argument. It is not lost — `#condition` stringifies
the whole expression, so it still prints — but it is not doing what it looks like it is doing.)

---

**2. `complex_tensor` — no shape validation in Release, and the wrong shape kind in Debug.**

```cpp
// complex.cpp:33-36
ComplexTensor complex_tensor(const Tensor& real, const Tensor& imag) {
    TT_ASSERT(real.padded_shape() == imag.padded_shape(), "Tensor shapes of real and imag should be identical");
    return ComplexTensor({real, imag});
}
```

Two problems stacked:

- In Release there is no check at all, so a mismatched pair is accepted and the mismatch surfaces
  later, inside whichever complex op consumes it.
- Even in Debug it compares `padded_shape()`. Two tensors with *different logical shapes* that pad
  to the same tile extent — logical `[1,1,32,50]` and `[1,1,32,60]`, both padding to
  `[1,1,32,64]` — satisfy the assertion while being semantically different shapes. The message says
  "Tensor shapes ... should be identical", which is the logical claim, so the comparison does not
  test what the message states.

Both are addressed by the same change:

```cpp
-    TT_ASSERT(real.padded_shape() == imag.padded_shape(), "Tensor shapes of real and imag should be identical");
+    TT_FATAL(real.logical_shape() == imag.logical_shape(),
+             "complex_tensor requires identical real/imag shapes, got {} and {}",
+             real.logical_shape(), imag.logical_shape());
```

This is the same logical-vs-padded confusion as #53277, #53283 and #53284, which is why I am
mentioning it here rather than filing it separately.

---

**3. `mac` — lowest severity, listed for completeness.**

```cpp
// ternary_composite_op.cpp:173-175
// all scalars
TT_ASSERT(a_is_scalar && b_is_scalar && c_is_scalar);
return ttnn::add(ttnn::multiply(a, b), c);
```

This sits at the end of an if-chain that has already handled every other combination, so the
condition is close to tautological and dropping it in Release costs little. It also carries no
message. Flagging it only so a sweep does not have to rediscover it; I would not fix this one on
its own.

### Expected

Input validation on a public API should hold in the builds people actually run. `TT_FATAL` is the
mechanism already used for this throughout the same files — `polyval`'s neighbours in
`binary_composite_op.cpp` use `TT_FATAL` for their argument checks — so this is a consistency fix
rather than a new convention.

Concretely: `polyval` should reject an empty `coeffs` with a clear error instead of reading out of
bounds; `complex_tensor` should reject mismatched logical shapes; `mac`'s assert can stay or go.

### Steps to reproduce

I do not have a Tenstorrent card, and the point of this report is that the behaviour differs by
build type, so the repro needs a **Release** build.

```python
import ttnn, torch
device = ttnn.open_device(device_id=0)
x = ttnn.from_torch(torch.randn((1, 1, 32, 32)), dtype=ttnn.bfloat16,
                    layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device)

# 1. polyval with no coefficients — expect a clean error, currently UB in Release
try:
    print(ttnn.polyval(x, []))
except Exception as e:
    print("polyval raised (good):", e)

# 2. complex_tensor with mismatched logical shapes that share a padded shape
a = ttnn.from_torch(torch.randn((1, 1, 32, 50)), dtype=ttnn.bfloat16,
                    layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device)
b = ttnn.from_torch(torch.randn((1, 1, 32, 60)), dtype=ttnn.bfloat16,
                    layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device)
try:
    ttnn.complex_tensor(a, b)
    print("complex_tensor accepted mismatched shapes (bad)")
except Exception as e:
    print("complex_tensor raised (good):", e)

ttnn.close_device(device)
```

A correct implementation raises on both. Today, in Release, the first is undefined behaviour and
the second is accepted silently. In a Debug build the first raises and the second still passes,
because of the padded-shape comparison.

### Why the current tests do not catch it

- CI runs and the sweeps pass valid arguments; no test calls `polyval` with an empty vector or
  `complex_tensor` with mismatched shapes, so the negative path is unexercised.
- Any test that did would likely run against a Debug build, where the `polyval` assert fires and
  the defect looks handled.

### Is this a regression?

No, and I did not bisect. All three are present at the SHA below. Context: `TT_ASSERT` is used
correctly elsewhere for genuine internal invariants — the issue is specifically its use on
caller-supplied arguments at a public boundary.

### Software Versions

| | |
|---|---|
| tt-metal | `main`, source as of 2026-08-16 |

### Hardware Details

No Tenstorrent card and no ttsim run — this is source analysis, and none of it needs hardware:
the `TT_ASSERT` Release expansion is at `tt_stl/tt_stl/assert.hpp:163-168`, and the three call
sites are at the lines quoted. The `coeffs[0]` read on an empty vector follows from the control
flow above it. What I have not done is execute a Release build to observe the UB, which by its
nature may present as anything.

### Impact

`polyval` is the one with real teeth: undefined behaviour reachable from user input in the build
configuration everyone ships. The others are correctness-of-validation rather than crashes.
Grouped into one report because the root cause is shared and a fix is a single small pass.

items.title: prod_bw passes padded_shape bounds to ttnn::slice (which resolves logically) and compares logical_shape against padded_shape in its guard
items.body:
### Component / Area

ttnn eltwise unary backward — `ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/unary_backward/unary_backward.cpp`, `prod_bw` (the `dim`-specified path, `all_dimensions == false`)

### Issue Type (optional)

Bad Outputs

### Observed

`prod_bw` mixes logical and padded shapes in two places on the same path. I want to be precise
about which half I can prove from source and which half I cannot, so they are separated below.

**1. The guard compares a logical shape against a padded shape.**

```cpp
// unary_backward.cpp:1682
if (prod_result.logical_shape() != grad.padded_shape()) {
```

These are different quantities by definition, so the comparison does not test what it reads as
testing. For a tile-aligned `grad` they happen to coincide and the test behaves; for any `grad`
whose logical extent is not a tile multiple they differ purely because of padding. Given
`prod_result` comes from `ttnn::prod(input, dim, keepdim=true)`, its logical shape carries a `1`
in the reduced dimension, so in the reducing case the two are essentially never equal and the
branch is taken unconditionally — the guard is not selecting anything. Either way it is comparing
the wrong pair; the honest reading is that one side should be `grad.logical_shape()`.

**2. Padded coordinates are handed to `ttnn::slice`, which resolves against the logical shape.**

```cpp
// dim == 3 / -1
ttsl::SmallVector<uint32_t> end_index = {
    grad.padded_shape()[0], 1, grad.padded_shape()[1], grad.padded_shape()[2]};
Tensor new_slice_tensor = ttnn::slice(required, start_index, end_index, step, std::nullopt);

// dim == 2 / -2 — same shape of bug
ttsl::SmallVector<uint32_t> end_index = {
    grad.padded_shape()[0], 1, grad.padded_shape()[1], grad.padded_shape()[3]};
```

`ttnn::slice` takes its bounds against `input_tensor.logical_shape()` (`slice.cpp:95`) and maps
them through `wrap_index(index, input_shape[i])` with `input_shape` logical
(`slice.cpp:222-223`). `wrap_index` is

```cpp
// data_movement/common/common.cpp:486
uint32_t wrap_index(int index, int size) { return index < 0 ? size + index : index; }
```

which normalises negative indices only — a positive bound past the logical extent passes through
unchanged. The sole downstream assertion is `modified_ends[i] >= modified_begins[i]`
(`slice.cpp:344`); there is no upper-bound check. The output extent is computed as `end - begin`,
so a padded bound silently yields an oversized slice that reads tile padding as data rather than
raising.

This is the same mechanism as #53283 (`split_tensor_for_glu`), in a different file and a
different op — a fix to either does not reach the other.

### What I could not determine

I have not established the exact numeric output. `prod_bw` chains `permute` → `slice` →
`permute` → `bcast`, and the trailing `bcast(reciprocal_input, temp, MUL, W/H)` may or may not
re-broadcast over the oversized extent in a way that masks or compounds it. Predicting the final
tensor would mean modelling those four ops together, which I am not willing to assert without
running it.

So the claim here is narrower than my other reports: **the bounds handed to `slice` are padded
where `slice` expects logical, and the guard compares mismatched shape kinds.** Both are visible
in the source and neither depends on hardware. Whether that surfaces as wrong gradient values, a
wrong shape, or is absorbed downstream is exactly what a run would settle, and I would rather say
so than guess.

### Expected

`prod_bw` should use `grad.logical_shape()` for the slice bounds and compare like against like in
the guard, matching `torch.prod`'s backward semantics, which are defined on logical extents with
no notion of tile padding.

```cpp
-    if (prod_result.logical_shape() != grad.padded_shape()) {
+    if (prod_result.logical_shape() != grad.logical_shape()) {
...
-        end_index = {grad.padded_shape()[0], 1, grad.padded_shape()[1], grad.padded_shape()[2]};
+        end_index = {grad.logical_shape()[0], 1, grad.logical_shape()[1], grad.logical_shape()[2]};
```

and the same substitution in the `dim == 2 / -2` branch.

### Steps to reproduce

I do not have a Tenstorrent card. These are the commands for someone who does. The shapes matter:
the last two dimensions must not be tile multiples, so that logical and padded differ.

```python
import torch
import ttnn

device = ttnn.open_device(device_id=0)

for shape in [(1, 1, 50, 100), (1, 1, 32, 100), (1, 1, 32, 128)]:   # last one is the control
    x = torch.rand(shape, dtype=torch.bfloat16) + 0.5      # keep away from zero, prod_bw divides
    g = torch.randn(shape, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    xt = x.clone().float().requires_grad_(True)
    torch.prod(xt, dim=3, keepdim=True).backward(
        torch.prod(xt, dim=3, keepdim=True).detach() * 0 + g.float().sum(dim=3, keepdim=True))
    tx = ttnn.from_torch(x, dtype=ttnn.bfloat16, layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device)
    tg = ttnn.from_torch(g, dtype=ttnn.bfloat16, layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device)
    out = ttnn.to_torch(ttnn.from_device(ttnn.prod_bw(tg, tx, dim=3)[0]))
    print(f"{shape}: ttnn {tuple(out.shape)} vs input {tuple(x.shape)} "
          f"{'ok' if out.shape == x.shape else 'SHAPE MISMATCH'}")

ttnn.close_device(device)
```

The gradient of `prod` w.r.t. its input has the input's shape, so a shape mismatch on the first two
rows and a match on `(1, 1, 32, 128)` would confirm the padded-bounds path. If the shapes all
match, the slice is being absorbed downstream and the report reduces to the guard being a
type confusion — still worth fixing, but not a bad-output bug.

### Why the current tests do not catch it

- The `prod_bw` sweeps and unit tests use tile-aligned shapes, so `logical_shape() ==
  padded_shape()` throughout and both defects are inert.
- #14886 ("ttnn.prod_bw - Low PCC", closed) exercised accuracy on aligned shapes; nothing samples
  a width or height between tile boundaries.

### Is this a regression?

No, and I did not bisect. Both reads are present at the SHA below. Context rather than blame: the
same logical/padded confusion appears in `_variance_impl` (#53277) and `split_tensor_for_glu`
(#53283), which suggests a shared habit from before the logical/padded distinction was
consistently drawn, rather than three unrelated slips.

### Software Versions

| | |
|---|---|
| tt-metal | `main`, source as of 2026-08-16 |
| reference | `torch.prod` backward semantics (logical extents) |

### Hardware Details

No Tenstorrent card and no ttsim run.

The two source facts — padded bounds into a logical-resolving `slice`, and the mismatched-kind
comparison — are read directly from `unary_backward.cpp`, `slice.cpp` and `common.cpp` at the
lines quoted. The non-clamping behaviour of `wrap_index` and the absence of an upper-bound assert
in `slice` I verified while investigating #53283. The downstream consequence is explicitly left
open above rather than asserted.

### Impact

`prod_bw` is not on a hot training path for most models, so I would not rate this urgent. It is
filed because the mechanism is confirmed and shared with #53283, and because a gradient that is
silently wrong on some shapes and right on others is the kind of defect that costs a great deal of
time to attribute if it does bite.

items.title: ttnn.lerp uses the unbranched form, so lerp(a, b, 1.0) does not return b (33.8% of sampled pairs); torch.lerp branches to keep the endpoint
items.body:
### Component / Area

ttnn eltwise ternary — `ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/ternary/ternary_composite_op.cpp` (`_lerp`, `_lerp_overload`)

### Issue Type (optional)

Bad Outputs

### Observed

`ttnn.lerp` evaluates the interpolation in the single naive form, for both the scalar-weight and
tensor-weight overloads:

```cpp
// _lerp_overload  (scalar weight)
Tensor t_diff = ttnn::subtract(end, input, ...);
Tensor t_mul  = ttnn::multiply(t_diff, weight, ...);
Tensor result = ttnn::add(input, t_mul, ...);

// _lerp  (tensor weight) — same arithmetic, fused
Tensor t_diff = ttnn::multiply(ttnn::subtract(end, input, ...), weight, ...);
Tensor result = ttnn::add(input, t_diff, ...);
```

Its registered golden is `torch.lerp`, which does not use that form unconditionally. PyTorch
branches on the weight (`aten/src/ATen/native/Lerp.h`):

```cpp
return (std::abs(weight_val) < scalar_t(0.5))
    ? self_val + weight_val * (end_val - self_val)
    : end_val - (end_val - self_val) * (scalar_t(1) - weight_val);
```

The second branch is anchored at `end` rather than at `self`, and it exists precisely so that the
`w -> 1` side of the interval keeps its endpoint. `ttnn.lerp` only ever evaluates the first branch.

**The consequence that is not a tolerance question: `lerp(a, b, 1.0)` does not return `b`.**

At `w = 1` the golden's branch reduces to `end - (end - self) * 0`, which is exactly `end` for any
finite inputs. The naive form computes `a + 1.0 * (b - a)`, and `a + (b - a)` is not `b` in
floating point once `b - a` has been rounded.

Sampling 200,000 random `(a, b)` pairs in `float32` with exponents spanning `1e-20` to `1e20`,
`a + 1.0*(b-a) != b` on **67,661 of them — 33.8%**. Examples:

| a | b | `ttnn.lerp(a, b, 1.0)` | `torch.lerp(a, b, 1.0)` |
|---|---|---|---|
| -3.421972e-05 | 5.681e-05 | 5.6810004e-05 | 5.681e-05 |
| -6.487227e+14 | 3.576148e+14 | 3.57614815e+14 | 3.576148e+14 |
| 1.47551e-20 | -1.522223e-20 | -1.52222316e-20 | -1.522223e-20 |
| -0.000710318 | 0.0009918796 | 0.000991879497 | 0.0009918796 |

`lerp(a, b, 0.0)` is unaffected — the naive form gives `a + 0*(b-a) = a` exactly — so only the
upper endpoint is lost. An interpolation primitive that does not reproduce its own endpoints is
the thing the branch in the reference is there to prevent.

**Away from the endpoint the divergence is about 1 ulp**, and I want to be straight that this half
is a tolerance argument rather than a correctness one. Over 400,000 random `(a, b, w)` triples with
`w` in `[0, 1]`, `ttnn.lerp` differs from `torch.lerp` on 21.25%, with relative differences around
`1e-7` — one `float32` ulp. Sample rows:

| a | b | w | ttnn | torch | rel |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| -8.1174e+13 | 1.65576e+13 | 0.909704 | 7.73283696e+12 | 7.73283801e+12 | 1.4e-07 |
| 8.89362e-16 | -5.18033e-17 | 0.664152 | 2.64284973e-16 | 2.64285053e-16 | 3.0e-07 |
| -4.30809e+07 | -2.28417e+07 | 0.668653 | -29547908 | -29547910 | 6.8e-08 |

One thing I checked and did **not** find, stated so nobody re-derives it: the naive form does not
produce results outside `[min(a,b), max(a,b)]`. Zero violations in 400,000 samples. The overshoot
one might expect from the unanchored form does not materialise; the endpoint identity is the real
casualty.

### Expected

`ttnn.lerp(a, b, 1.0)` should equal `b` exactly, in `float32` and `bfloat16`, for every finite
`a, b` — matching the registered golden, which gets this by construction rather than by rounding
luck. `lerp(a, b, 0.0) == a` already holds and should stay.

The direct fix is to mirror the reference's branch: use `a + w*(b-a)` for `|w| < 0.5` and
`b - (b-a)*(1-w)` otherwise. On the scalar-weight overload the branch is free — `weight` is a host
value, so the choice is made once on the host and only one composition is ever built. On the
tensor-weight overload it costs a `where` over the two forms, which is the same shape as the
existing `where`-based special-case handling elsewhere in the eltwise composites.

### Steps to reproduce

I do not have a Tenstorrent card. These are the commands for someone who does.

```python
import torch
import ttnn

device = ttnn.open_device(device_id=0)

pairs = [(-3.421972e-05, 5.681e-05), (-6.487227e14, 3.576148e14),
         (1.47551e-20, -1.522223e-20), (-0.000710318, 0.0009918796)]

print(f"{'a':>16} {'b':>16} {'ttnn w=1':>18} {'exact b':>18}  ok")
for a, b in pairs:
    ta = ttnn.from_torch(torch.full((1, 1, 32, 32), a, dtype=torch.float32),
                         dtype=ttnn.float32, layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device)
    tb = ttnn.from_torch(torch.full((1, 1, 32, 32), b, dtype=torch.float32),
                         dtype=ttnn.float32, layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device)
    got = ttnn.to_torch(ttnn.from_device(ttnn.lerp(ta, tb, 1.0)))[0, 0, 0, 0].item()
    print(f"{a:>16.9g} {b:>16.9g} {got:>18.9g} {b:>18.9g}  {'ok' if got == b else 'FAIL'}")

ttnn.close_device(device)
```

A correct implementation prints `ok` on every row.

### Why the current tests do not catch it

- `tests/sweep_framework/sweeps/eltwise/ternary/lerp/` draws its weight from a random uniform
  distribution, so `w` is never exactly `1.0` — the endpoint is not a sampled point, and with
  probability one it never will be.
- The comparison is PCC-based. A 1-ulp difference on 21% of elements does not move PCC, so the
  general divergence is invisible to it as well.
- No test asserts the endpoint identities `lerp(a,b,0) == a` and `lerp(a,b,1) == b`, which is the
  cheapest oracle available for this op and needs no reference implementation at all.

### Is this a regression?

No. Both overloads have used the naive form at the SHA below and I did not bisect. Worth noting
that #47080 (closed) asked whether `ttnn.lerp` was *more* numerically accurate than a hand-rolled
combiner in `tt_dit`; this is the concrete answer to the shape of that question, and it is the
other way round from what one would assume from the name.

### Software Versions

| | |
|---|---|
| tt-metal | `main`, source as of 2026-08-15 |
| reference | `torch.lerp` per the registered golden in `ttnn/ttnn/operations/ternary.py` |

### Hardware Details

No Tenstorrent card and no ttsim run — saying so up front.

The composition is read from the source. The failure rates and the tables come from evaluating
both formulas in `float32` with each intermediate rounded to `float32` — the same subtract,
multiply and add the composite performs, in the same order. That models host-side composition of
`float32` element-wise ops, which is what these two functions build; it does not model any SFPU
rounding behaviour that might differ on silicon. The endpoint claim is the robust one, since it
follows from `a + (b-a) != b` in any IEEE-754 binary format and does not depend on the accumulator.
A run of the repro would confirm the rates.

### Impact

Low severity and I would not argue otherwise — one ulp, on an op that is not on a hot model path.
It is filed because the endpoint case is exact rather than approximate: code that interpolates to
`w = 1` and expects to land on `end`, or a test asserting that identity, gets a value that is
merely close. That is cheap to fix on the scalar overload, where the branch costs nothing at
runtime.

items.title: ttnn.lcm accepts int32 but the kernel assumes 15-bit operands: gcd_body<15> where gcd uses <31>, and a u16 final multiply
items.body:
### Component / Area

SFPU kernels — `tt_metal/hw/ckernels/{blackhole,wormhole_b0}/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_lcm.h` (`calculate_sfpu_lcm`), reached from `ttnn.lcm`

### Issue Type (optional)

Bad Outputs

### Observed

`ttnn.lcm` accepts the full `int32` range and is implemented on two internal assumptions that
only hold for roughly 15-bit operands. Neither is enforced anywhere, and neither produces a
diagnostic when violated — the op returns a wrong integer.

**1. The GCD sub-computation is given half the iterations it needs.**

`calculate_sfpu_lcm` calls the shared binary-GCD body with a 15-bit budget:

```cpp
// ckernel_sfpu_lcm.h
// Binary GCD algorithm; assumes abs(a) < 2^15 and abs(b) < 2^15, hence gcd(a, b) < 2^15
calculate_sfpu_gcd_body<15>();
```

while `ttnn.gcd`, on the same inputs, uses the full budget:

```cpp
// ckernel_sfpu_gcd.h, calculate_sfpu_gcd
calculate_sfpu_gcd_body<31>();
```

The template parameter *is* the iteration count — `int iterations = max_input_bits - 1`, replayed
seven instructions at a time. `gcd_body<31>` runs 30 iterations, which the body's own comment
justifies as the worst case for 31-bit inputs. `gcd_body<15>` runs 14. For operands at or above
`2^15` the loop exits before the algorithm has converged, and whatever is left in `LREG1` is used
as the GCD.

**2. The final product is a 16×16→32 multiply.**

```cpp
// Finally, compute lcm(a, b) = a/gcd(a, b) * b
calculate_sfpu_mul_u16_to_u32_body();
```

That helper is `SFPMUL24` taken as an upper/lower pair — a `u16 * u16 -> u32` product. It requires
both `a/gcd(a,b)` and `b` to fit in 16 bits. `a/gcd` is only bounded by `a`, so it exceeds 16 bits
whenever `a` is large and the two operands are coprime, even when the LCM itself is a small
`int32`.

**Nothing constrains the inputs.** `ttnn::lcm` in `binary_composite_op.cpp` forwards straight to
`invoke_binary_ng` with no range validation, and the dispatch rule admits the whole type:

```cpp
// binary_ng_device_operation.cpp, is_binary_sfpu_op
case LCM:
case GCD: return (a == INT32 && b == INT32);
```

So the declared domain is `int32` and the implemented domain is about `[-2^15, 2^15]`.

### Cases

Every row below has an LCM that is an ordinary `int32`, far from any representable limit:

| a | b | lcm(a, b) | a/gcd | why it should fail |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 65536 | 3 | 196,608 | 65,536 | `a/gcd` needs 17 bits — defect 2 |
| 999983 | 2 | 1,999,966 | 999,983 | `a/gcd` needs 20 bits — defect 2 |
| 786432 | 1310720 | 3,932,160 | 3 | both operands ≥ 2^15 — defect 1 |
| 100000 | 150000 | 300,000 | 2 | both operands ≥ 2^15 — defect 1 |
| 40000 | 60000 | 120,000 | 2 | both operands ≥ 2^15 — defect 1 |
| 1048576 | 262144 | 1,048,576 | 4 | both operands ≥ 2^15 — defect 1 |
| 30000 | 21000 | 210,000 | 10 | control — both under 2^15, should pass |

`lcm(65536, 3)` is the cleanest single case: the answer is 196,608, and the only reason it cannot
be produced is that the implementation forms `65536 * 3` in a 16-bit lane.

### Expected

`ttnn.lcm` should agree with `torch.lcm` — its registered golden — for every input pair whose LCM
is representable in `int32`, or it should reject the inputs it cannot handle. Returning a silently
wrong integer is the one outcome that should not happen.

Note the asymmetry that makes this worth fixing rather than documenting: `lcm(a, b) <= a * b`
only in the coprime case. For operands sharing a large factor the LCM is small — `lcm(2^20, 2^20)`
is `2^20` — so the 15-bit restriction is far tighter than representability of the result requires.
A great many `int32` pairs have a perfectly ordinary LCM and are outside the implemented domain.

For defect 1 the fix is a one-token change, `gcd_body<15>` to `gcd_body<31>`, at the cost of the
extra replay iterations. For defect 2 the product needs enough width for `a/gcd`, or the operand
order needs to be chosen so the smaller cofactor goes into the 16-bit lane — `a/gcd * b` and
`b/gcd * a` are both valid factorisations of the LCM, and picking the one whose cofactor is
smaller widens the working range for free.

If the 15-bit domain is instead intended, then it should be enforced on the host with a clear
error, and stated in the `ttnn.lcm` docs, which today say nothing about a range restriction.

### Steps to reproduce

I do not have a Tenstorrent card. These are the commands for someone who does.

```python
import torch
import ttnn

device = ttnn.open_device(device_id=0)

pairs = [(65536, 3), (999983, 2), (786432, 1310720), (100000, 150000),
         (40000, 60000), (1048576, 262144), (30000, 21000)]

print(f"{'a':>10} {'b':>10} {'ttnn':>14} {'torch':>14}  ok")
for a, b in pairs:
    ta = ttnn.from_torch(torch.full((1, 1, 32, 32), a, dtype=torch.int32),
                         dtype=ttnn.int32, layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device)
    tb = ttnn.from_torch(torch.full((1, 1, 32, 32), b, dtype=torch.int32),
                         dtype=ttnn.int32, layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device)
    got = ttnn.to_torch(ttnn.from_device(ttnn.lcm(ta, tb)))[0, 0, 0, 0].item()
    want = torch.lcm(torch.tensor(a), torch.tensor(b)).item()
    print(f"{a:>10} {b:>10} {got:>14} {want:>14}  {'ok' if got == want else 'FAIL'}")

ttnn.close_device(device)
```

The last row is the control: both operands are under `2^15`, so it should pass in the same run
that the others fail, which separates this from any general breakage of the op.

### Why the current tests do not catch it

- `tests/sweep_framework/sweeps/eltwise/binary/lcm/lcm.py` draws both operands from
  `torch_random(low=-1024, high=1024)`. That is 11 bits — comfortably inside the implemented
  domain and nowhere near the 15-bit edge.
- The `gcd` sweep alongside it uses the same band, so the contrast between `gcd_body<31>` and
  `gcd_body<15>` never shows up: both are correct over `±1024`.
- #21182 ("Retest - gcd, lcm ops with appropriate configs", closed) re-ran these ops but did not
  widen the input range past the same band.

No test places an operand at or above `2^15`, which is why a restriction documented in a code
comment has never surfaced as a failure.

### Is this a regression?

No. The `<15>` budget is present at the SHA below and I did not bisect. Context rather than blame:
the kernel is contributed code (`SPDX-FileCopyrightText: © 2025 Jason Davies`), and the comment
naming the assumption is right above the call, so this reads as a deliberate narrowing for the
iteration cost that was never mirrored by a guard on the host side or a note in the docs.

### Software Versions

| | |
|---|---|
| tt-metal | `main`, source as of 2026-08-15 |
| reference | `torch.lcm`, the registered golden for `ttnn.lcm` |

Same code on Blackhole and Wormhole — the two `ckernel_sfpu_lcm.h` copies carry the identical
`gcd_body<15>` call and the identical `u16` multiply, so this is not architecture-specific.

### Hardware Details

No Tenstorrent card and no ttsim run — stating that up front rather than leaving it to be found.

The analysis is of the source: the `<15>` versus `<31>` template arguments and the iteration count
they expand to, the `u16 * u16 -> u32` helper used for the final product, the absence of any range
check in `ttnn::lcm`, and the `INT32` admission in `is_binary_sfpu_op`. The case table is exact
integer arithmetic — `math.gcd` and `a // g * b` — establishing that each listed LCM is an ordinary
`int32` and identifying which of the two defects each pair is positioned to trigger.

What I have not done is observe the wrong values. The claim that these inputs are *outside the
implemented domain* follows from the source. The claim that each therefore returns a *specific*
wrong integer does not, since an unconverged binary GCD leaves a value I have not modelled
instruction by instruction. Running the repro above would settle exactly which rows fail and what
they return, and I would rather have that than assert it.

### Impact

Silent and integer-valued, which is the awkward combination: no `inf`, no `NaN`, no assertion, just
a plausible-looking number. `lcm` is not on a hot model path, so the blast radius is small — but
anything using it for stride, tiling or period computation over realistic magnitudes is outside the
implemented domain, and the failure carries no signal that it happened.

items.title: global_avg_pool2d returns structurally wrong values on Blackhole for [1,7,7,2048] (PCC 0.55)
items.body:
## Summary

`test_run_average_pool[BFLOAT16-resnet50_unpadded]` fails its correlation check on Blackhole:

```
Passing PCC = False
Output PCC = 0.5478098686296509
```

`tests/tt_eager/python_api_testing/unit_testing/misc/test_average_pool.py::test_run_average_pool`, `act_shape = [1, 7, 7, 2048]`, `bfloat16`.

The value is bit-identical across runs, so this is deterministic rather than flaky. The sibling parameterisation in the same file (`tile_divisible`, `[1, 1, 32, 64]`) passes at PCC 0.9999984714740633, so `global_avg_pool2d` is not broken in general — it is specific to this shape.

## The output is structurally wrong, not mis-scaled

Worth stating up front because it rules out the obvious explanation. `shape_padded()` pads dim 2 from 7 to 32, so the tensor handed to the op is `[1, 7, 32, 2048]` with 25 zero columns, while the golden is computed on the unpadded `[1, 7, 7, 2048]`. If the op simply averaged over the padded extent, every channel would be scaled by the same 49/224 = 0.21875 and PCC would stay at 1.0, because Pearson correlation is scale-invariant.

Measured per-channel ratio of output to golden:

```
ratio   mean=2.263587   std=116.446693   min=-1134.297852   max=5111.541504
```

Individual channels also flip sign:

```
first 8 out    : -0.00800  -0.03809  -0.08887  +0.07910  +0.08301  -0.08398  -0.01746  +0.03418
first 8 golden : -0.06395  -0.02713  -0.12696  -0.00901  -0.13661  -0.18339  -0.08714  +0.10446
```

So the result is not the correct answer times a constant. Something in the padded path produces different values per channel.

## Reproduction

```bash
pytest tests/tt_eager/python_api_testing/unit_testing/misc/test_average_pool.py \
  -k "BFLOAT16-resnet50_unpadded" -xvvv
```

(or `scripts/run_safe_pytest.sh --run-all tests/tt_eager/python_api_testing/unit_testing/misc/test_average_pool.py -v`, which runs both parameterisations and shows the passing sibling alongside.)

## What has been ruled out

- **Not flaky.** Same PCC to the last digit across every run.
- **Not a scale/normalisation error.** Per-channel ratios vary by orders of magnitude and change sign (above).
- **Not DRAM harvesting.** The system this was found on has one GDDR channel harvested per chip; the test returns `0.5478098686296509` with 7 banks and the identical value with all 8 banks enabled, with no other change.
- **Not the op in general.** The tile-aligned parameterisation passes at 0.9999998.

## Possible direction

The one structural difference between the failing and passing cases is that the failing one goes through `pad_to_tile(0.0)`. Note that dim 2 here is a spatial dimension (the tensor is NHWC, so `[N, H, W, C]` and W is padded 7 to 32), and zero-padding a spatial dimension is not a no-op for average pooling. Whether the defect is that the op mishandles the padded region, or that padding metadata is not carried into the reduction, I have not determined — flagging it as the obvious place to look rather than as a diagnosis.

## Related

[#44002](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/issues/44002) is the same test in the same CI group, but a different symptom — a hard `TT_FATAL` about tile alignment after `global_avg_pool2d`, fixed and closed in May. This is a wrong-results failure, not a crash, so it is a separate problem on the same test.

[#6237](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/issues/6237) reported low PCC from `global_avg_pool2d` on Grayskull and is closed. No open issue matches low PCC on Blackhole.

## Environment

Blackhole, firmware 19.13.2, KMD 2.9.0. The test carries no architecture-specific handling, so it is expected to pass here.

items.title: test_update_cache.py hardcodes an 8-bank expected layout; fails on DRAM-harvested parts (runtime is correct)
items.body:
## Summary

`TestUpdateCacheWithKVPE::test_kvpe_cache_op` hardcodes the expected `TensorMemoryLayout` for each mesh shape, assuming 8 DRAM banks. On a device exposing fewer banks — for example a DRAM-harvested Blackhole such as P100a — the `HEIGHT_SHARDED` case fails:

```
AssertionError: Expected cache layout to be TensorMemoryLayout.HEIGHT_SHARDED,
                but got TensorMemoryLayout.ND_SHARDED
```

Three parameterisations fail (`fill`, `fill_cache_for_user`, `update`), all `[DataType.BFLOAT8_B-mesh_shape1-1024-128-HEIGHT_SHARDED]`.

**The runtime is behaving correctly here — only the test's expectation is wrong.** There is no data-correctness problem; `ND_SHARDED` is simply a different, valid layout.

## Why ND_SHARDED is the correct answer on fewer banks

A legacy `HEIGHT_SHARDED` spec requires at most one shard per core. `TensorSpec::compute_legacy_memory_config()` (`tt_metal/impl/tensor/spec/tensor_spec.cpp:364`) declines the conversion when that does not hold:

```cpp
// Check that the number of shards fits onto the cores
size_t total_num_shards = num_shards_along_height * num_shards_along_width;
if (total_num_shards > shard_spec.grid.num_cores()) {
    return std::nullopt;      // stays ND_SHARDED
}
```

This is deliberate — the neighbouring `CONTIGUOUS_1D` branch carries the comment *"Don't fabricate a (garbled) legacy spec — leave the tensor ND-sharding-only."* Refusing to invent a legacy layout that cannot represent the actual placement is the right behaviour.

Confirmed empirically. The rule is purely `num_shards <= num_banks`, independent of any specific bank count:

| Tensor shape | Shards | Bank grid | Resulting layout |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `[2,1,128,32]` | 8 | 8 | `HEIGHT_SHARDED` |
| `[2,1,128,32]` | 8 | 7 | `ND_SHARDED` |
| `[1,1,128,32]` | 4 | 7 | `HEIGHT_SHARDED` |
| `[1,1,128,32]` | 4 | 3 | `ND_SHARDED` |

(All with `shard_shape=[1,1,32,32]`, `ROUND_ROBIN_1D`, DRAM.) Note the third row: 4 shards on a 7-bank grid still normalises to `HEIGHT_SHARDED`, so this is not "the grid must be 8" — it is only whether the shards fit one per bank.

The model-side code is already harvest-aware and is not the problem: `init_kvpe_cache()` builds its grid from `get_num_dram_banks(mesh_device)`, whose docstring reads *"Full Blackhole = 8; harvested parts expose fewer (e.g. 7)."*

## The shard count in the comments is also wrong

`tests/tt_eager/python_api_testing/unit_testing/misc/test_update_cache.py:480`

```python
((8, 4), 1024, 128, "HEIGHT_SHARDED"),  # 128/32 = 4 shards across 8 banks → ≤1 shard/bank → HEIGHT_SHARDED
```

and the matching docstring at line 495. The real count is **8**, not 4: the cache is `[num_kvpe_cache_layers=2, 1, seq_len_local=128, 32]`, so the physical height is 2 × 128 = 256 and 256/32 = 8 shards. The layer dimension is omitted from the arithmetic.

This matters because it is exactly why the case is bank-count-critical. At the 4 shards the comment claims, the test would still pass on 7 banks (row 3 above). At the actual 8 shards it passes only when there are exactly 8 banks available.

## Suggested fix

Derive the expectation instead of hardcoding it, e.g.:

```python
num_banks = get_num_dram_banks(mesh_device)
num_shards = (num_kvpe_cache_layers * expected_seq_len_local) // NUM_CONTIGUOUS_TOKENS_IN_DRAM_BANK
expected_layout_enum = (
    ttnn.TensorMemoryLayout.HEIGHT_SHARDED if num_shards <= num_banks
    else ttnn.TensorMemoryLayout.ND_SHARDED
)
```

and correct the shard arithmetic in the parametrize comments and the docstring to include the layer dimension.

## Why CI does not catch it

`test_update_cache.py` sits in the `runtime_fd_python_*` groups, which run on `wh_n150_civ2` and `bh_p150b_civ2` only. `bh_p100a_civ2_viommu` appears in the `runtime_sd_*` groups and `service_core_manager`, but not in any group that runs this test, so it never executes on a DRAM-harvested part.

## Related

Same root cause class as #53264 (hardcoded 8-bank assumption in a test), but distinct in impact: that one exposes a genuine runtime validation gap and silently corrupts data, whereas this one is a wrong expectation over correct runtime behaviour.

## Environment

Blackhole, firmware 19.13.2, KMD 2.9.0, 7 of 8 DRAM banks available. All three cases pass when all 8 banks are enabled, with no other change.

items.title: test_reshard.py hardcodes an 8-bank DRAM shard grid; 6 cases silently compare wrong data on DRAM-harvested parts
items.body:
## Summary

`test_reshard.py` builds DRAM shard grids by hardcoding 8 banks, and guards that assumption against the wrong dimension. On any Blackhole exposing fewer than 8 DRAM banks — including DRAM-harvested parts such as P100a — this produces 16 failures, 6 of which silently compare wrong data rather than erroring.

The helper `_l1_dram_mem_config()` (`tests/tt_eager/python_api_testing/unit_testing/misc/test_reshard.py:1580`) handles the three sharding schemes inconsistently.

**The BLOCK_SHARDED branch is correct** — it asks the device (line 1592):

```python
num_dram_banks = device.dram_grid_size().x
dram_banks = ttnn.CoreRangeSet(
    [ttnn.CoreRange(ttnn.CoreCoord(b, 0), ttnn.CoreCoord(b, 0)) for b in range(num_dram_banks)]
)
```

**The HEIGHT_SHARDED and WIDTH_SHARDED branches hardcode 8** (lines 1604–1613):

```python
if scheme == ttnn.TensorMemoryLayout.HEIGHT_SHARDED:
    if grid_size.x < 8:
        pytest.skip("Device grid too small for 8-core height sharding")
    grid = ttnn.CoreRangeSet({ttnn.CoreRange(ttnn.CoreCoord(0, 0), ttnn.CoreCoord(7, 0))})
    shard_shape = (height // 8, width)
elif scheme == ttnn.TensorMemoryLayout.WIDTH_SHARDED:
    if grid_size.x < 8:
        pytest.skip("Device grid too small for 8-core width sharding")
    grid = ttnn.CoreRangeSet({ttnn.CoreRange(ttnn.CoreCoord(0, 0), ttnn.CoreCoord(7, 0))})
    shard_shape = (height, width // 8)
```

The guard checks `grid_size`, which is `device.compute_with_storage_grid_size()` (line 44) — the **compute** grid. That is comfortably wider than 8 on Blackhole, so the skip never fires. The grid is then used for **DRAM** sharding, where the bank count is what matters. With 7 banks, `CoreCoord(7, 0)` names a bank that does not exist.

## Impact

16 failures in two test functions — 11 in `test_reshard_between_L1_and_DRAM`, 5 in `test_reshard_dram_to_dram`. They split cleanly by which side DRAM is on:

| DRAM role | Result | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | `TT_FATAL @ metal_soc_descriptor.cpp:164` — "Logical DRAM core (7,0) is outside valid range (num_views=7)" | 9 |
| Source (row-major) | `TT_THROW @ allocator.cpp:352` — "No DRAM bank exists for core 7-0" | 1 |
| **Destination** | **no error — wrong data returned and compared** | **6** |

The six destination cases are the concerning ones. Nothing resolves the DRAM channel on the write path, so the write reports success:

| Case | Max ATOL Δ | Max RTOL Δ | PCC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `L1_HS-DRAM_WS-TILE-f32` | 0.9976 | 2685.99 | 0.8779 |
| `L1_WS-DRAM_HS-TILE-u16` | 2,133,167,616 | 1670.78 | 0.8757 |
| `L1_BS-DRAM_HS-TILE-f32` | 0.9904 | 2269.35 | 0.8766 |
| `DRAM_HS-L1_BS-TILE-bf16` | 0.9959 | 3326.69 | 0.8746 |
| `L1_WS-DRAM_HS-TILE-bf4_b` | 1.0 | inf | 0.8657 |
| (sixth) | — | — | 0.8742 |

PCC clusters tightly at 0.865–0.878 across dtypes, consistent with a systematic addressing error rather than sporadic corruption.

Note `DRAM_BS_nd-DRAM_HS-f32` also lands in the silent set — its *source* uses the correct `dram_grid_size()` branch while its *destination* uses the hardcoded 8, which is exactly what the pattern predicts.

Other DRAM reshard tests in the same file pass (`test_reshard_aligned_channels_height_sharded` with `BufferType.DRAM`, `test_reshard_diff_width`, `test_reshard_interleaved_to_block_sharded`), so DRAM resharding itself is fine — this is specific to the hardcoded grid.

## Why CI does not catch it

`test_reshard.py` lives in the `runtime_fd_python_*` groups, and those run on `wh_n150_civ2` and `bh_p150b_civ2` only:

```
runtime_fd_python_1 .. _7, _sweep    wh_n150_civ2, bh_p150b_civ2
```

`bh_p100a_civ2_viommu` appears in the `runtime_sd_*` groups and `service_core_manager`, but not in any group that runs this test. So the test never executes on a DRAM-harvested part in CI.

## Suggested fix

Derive the grid from the DRAM grid, matching what the BLOCK_SHARDED branch already does:

```python
num_dram_banks = device.dram_grid_size().x
grid = ttnn.CoreRangeSet({ttnn.CoreRange(ttnn.CoreCoord(0, 0), ttnn.CoreCoord(num_dram_banks - 1, 0))})
shard_shape = (height // num_dram_banks, width)   # and width // num_dram_banks for WIDTH_SHARDED
```

The shard shapes divide by 8 as well, so those need the same treatment; the test dimensions may need adjusting to stay divisible by a non-power-of-two bank count.

Note the guard should also move from `compute_with_storage_grid_size()` to the DRAM grid regardless of how the grid itself is derived — checking the compute grid to validate a DRAM assumption is the root mistake here.

## Related

The runtime does not currently reject an out-of-range DRAM shard grid, which is why 6 of these corrupt silently instead of erroring. #53263 adds that validation in `validate_buffer_parameters()`. With that change all 16 become clean errors at buffer creation, so the two fixes are complementary — and after #53263 lands, this test will fail loudly on harvested parts rather than half-passing.

## Environment

Blackhole, firmware 19.13.2, KMD 2.9.0, 7 of 8 DRAM banks available.
